en: Preface to the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*, composed by the disciple Ze’an.

Regarding the thirteen characters of the title below the name "Tan," they follow the brief explanation in the preface to the commentary; there is no need for a redundant or elaborate interpretation, as it merely follows the sequence of the title.
The titles of the ten chapters of the *Karmavācanā* differ slightly [from those in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*].
The commentary by the person from Jingzhou (the capital) is titled "General Preface" (*Tongshe xuwen*), which shares the same title as the ten chapters themselves.
Jingzhao was the capital where he resided; thus, with Fufeng to the left, Fengyi to the right, and Jingzhao in the center, these constitute the Three Commanderies (*Sanfu*).
"Jing" (京) means "great," and "zhao" (兆) means "multitude. It refers to the fact that the Son of Heaven must reside in a settlement where a great multitude dwells;
hence it is called Jingzhao.

"Chongyi" (崇義)—that is, "Venerating Righteousness"—is a specific designation for a *gārala* (monastery). This is because a wife, out of gratitude and righteousness toward her husband, donated her residence to become a temple.

Because of its great importance, it is called Chongyi Temple; it is so named because those who manage affairs succeed one another within it, as it was originally the residence of a local high minister.
The Sanskrit term *saṃghārāma* is translated here as "Garden of the Assembly.
Because Kāśyapa Mātanga came from afar to transmit the Dharma to the Han court, he was invited to reside at the Honglu Temple; thereafter, all monastic dwellings were referred to as "temples" (*si*).
"Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning one who diligently practices the cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Śākya" is fully called Śākyamuni, which means "Able Benevolent One"; this is the clan name of our Buddha’s distant ancestor. All [who follow] emerge from this.
The term "family" (kula) refers collectively to those of the Śākya clan; it is said that the four rivers, upon entering the ocean, no longer retain their distinct names.

Likewise, members of the four castes who have left the household life are all collectively called Śākyas. Since all who have left the household life are termed *śramaṇa*, the word "Śākya" is used to distinguish them from non-Buddhist *śramaṇas*.
Furthermore, because there are those within the Śākya clan who do not leave the household life, the term "*śramaṇa*" is used to further distinguish them. This is explained in detail as follows:
Regarding the explanations in the *Dàchāo Zhāngjì* (Chapter Notes of the Great Digest):
Daoxuan is the name of the patriarch; "Fǎbiàn" is also explained as usual.
The compiler has likely gathered the texts of the ten chapters of the *Karmavācanā* sacred teachings to compose this work.
The "Great Hero" (Mahāvīra) refers to the World-Honored One; because his cultivation, realization, transformation, and guidance are all "great," how could he not be a "heroic and valiant" one?

Thus, the World-Honored One is called the Great Heroic Valiant One. When the capacities of sentient beings have matured, he descends from Tuṣita to preside over the Sahā world, just as a sovereign presides over the universe.
The underlying intention of the World-Honored One’s descent to transform sentient beings is that "one person" refers to the Buddha himself.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "I desire to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself. Furthermore, the Commentary says:
"The Great Sage descended to first open the foundation of transformation, intending to rescue and deliver those in the realms of existence so that they may together ascend to the other shore."

The Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) comprehensively encompasses the temporal teachings of a single dispensation; "receiving the mandate" (*yingqi*) refers to this. "One Principle" (*yili*) indicates the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle’s perfect and sudden teaching.

Since the World-Honored One expounded the net of the Three Piṭaka teachings, those who received the mandate and were entrusted with the essential timing all desired that sentient beings, through diverse paths, return to manifest the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle’s perfection.
Therefore, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* states: "The water of the Dharma is one."
Rivers, streams, wells, and ponds differ only in their distinctions; my mind, however, is the mind of the inversion of self and person.
Therefore, the following provides medicine according to the illness.
Furthermore, the subsequent section clarifies the sequence of diagnosing the illness and administering the medicine.
The method of settling the mind by downward pressure is the source of the medicine; the slaying of the thieves of the five desires must proceed from clear wisdom.
Binding with concentration and grasping with precepts constitute the sequence of the three trainings, for which the precepts serve as the source.

This citation below is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. "Two tracks" refers to the path; marking the beginning with the single fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa* serves to highlight the preeminent leader of "abiding in observance.
Regarding the major sections, the single fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* constitutes the general course for "performing observance.

"Later followers and junior students" refers to those who have come after and those still learning, while "former practitioners and distant worthies" refers to the sages of antiquity. Although they are worthies and juniors, [they represent] the past and the present.
The *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* and the *Karmavācanā* constitute the essential and subtle core of the myriad practices of our shared school;
these are precisely the methods of the *śīla-dharma* and *karma*.
Therefore, the following citations serve as proof of what we uphold.
From this point downward, the Buddha’s wisdom was like the sun suddenly appearing in the Western Land; this was the time of his *nirvāṇa*.
The "Dharma-water" refers to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, which can wash away the defilements of the minds of sentient beings, and is thus metaphorically likened to water.
Its flowing from the West to the East Han corresponds to the period one thousand years after the extinction [of the Buddha].

In the Age of Decline (*śāsana-patana-kāla*), people were pure; in the Age of Semblance (*pratirūpaka-kāla*), people became coarse. The Southern Mountain [School] appeared during the final period of the Age of Semblance. The period following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is divided into three:

the first five hundred years constitute the Age of True Dharma (*saddharma*); the next five hundred years constitute the Middle Age; and the subsequent period, including the time of the Tang dynasty, constitutes the Final Age.

The two schools refer to the Sthavira (Theravāda) and Mahāsāṃghika schools; as for the eighteen or twenty schools, they represent the branches that have diverged from the root while retaining only the peripheral.
The *Pañcaśata-jñāna-śāstra* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five hundred distinct schools arose, asserting that ultimate emptiness is like a knife wounding the heart and so forth.
At the end, it says, "Then, the many blades descend"; from this point onward, the authors of treatises in both the eastern and western lands each followed their own particular school.
It is understood that these all represent the mutual elevation of various "pikes" (鋒).
From the individual divisions below up to the mutual elevation of the various pikes, there are those who have attained awakening to the Way, ensuring that the True Dharma does not fall to the ground.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Because of these differing characteristics, they associate in groups, transmitting [the teachings] to one another while engaging in mutual debate."
All have fully awakened to the Way and so forth.

However, although it is said below that [the teaching] has declined and fallen, the Way relies on people for its propagation; since those people have been lost, there are aspects of its Dharma that are no longer expounded.
Consequently, the flowing stream has no means to clarify itself, and the summit has no means to be rectified. This is surely because the Great Master...

The following passage, which begins with "Seizing upon the arising," serves as the preface for this composition. From the ancient times of the Cao-Wei dynasty down to the end of the Tang era, these works gradually increased in volume;
yet despite the great number of scrolls, they were all produced from the mere imagination of their authors without personal consultation of the original texts.

Consequently, the vast scope of the sacred teachings was reduced to what had been transmitted by predecessors through hearsay. Thus, before any critical examination of the fundamental sources was conducted, every thread of the tradition became reliant solely on conjecture.
Because they are empty, they lack any fundamental basis;
following their own minds, they do not obey the sacred teachings below. I respectfully recite [these words], yet I do not fathom the Buddha’s principles.

Such people are witnessed by the world, hence it is said they are "not few" and even "extremely many. Their arrogance and contempt are such that the penal laws cannot reach them, for they are ignorant and have not studied.
Regarding "faults" (*doṣa*), "sameness" refers to [the view that] they are identical; "difference" refers to looking at them from different perspectives.

Alternatively, while one might share the same right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) as others, because one does not wish to be the same as them, it is said that "all strive for equality. Previously, because one did not examine one's own faults, it was called "clinging to correctness";

however, this merely refers to what was heard previously, hence it is called "clinging to the past," which describes [the former state]. Alternatively, it may mean that the mind clings to the words of people of the past.

Because one considers oneself right, it is said, "He can reflect upon the past. If the character *yú* (隅) were instead written as *chí* (癡, foolish), it would mean that he was not merely foolish in the past, but perhaps foolish even now.

Furthermore, it says, "His delusion and confusion increase further. If this were interpreted by taking *yú* to mean a corner (*yǎojué*), it would imply that one can "reflect upon the other three corners" based on one;
however, this [person] is unable to take one case as an example for the others, which is likewise a reproach for his folly.
[The character] "ye" (this interpretation seems not to accord with the meaning of the text). "Qiandi" (潜地) means to sink and become hidden; it refers to falling to the ground.
Therefore, the citation below serves as proof for the meaning that when one does not follow the holy teachings, the Dharma sinks and falls. It is not like the "white dharma" (*śukladharma*);

"not relying on the white dharma" refers to [acts such as] performing white deeds and so forth. "Cigao" (慈誥) refers to the Buddha’s words. The *Shiming* (釋名) states: "To issue a command from above to those below is called 'gao' (誥)."
"Gao" means "to awaken"; it refers to awakening and realizing the intent of one's own mind. Regarding "Guanfu": "Guan" refers to the territory of Yongzhou within the passes;
"Fu" refers to the Three Fu, namely Left Fufeng, Right Fengyi, and Central Jingzhao. These Three Fu were established as the royal domain (Wangji).
The "Jùluó" (具羅) section below consists of thirty chapters; thus, the preface to the *Chāo* states: "However, as matters and objects are truly numerous, it is extremely difficult to categorize them.
Now, by grouping items according to their common nature to establish titles, I encompass various categories to form these thirty chapters.
Within them, the diverse manifestations of generating goodness and extinguishing evil are fully contained throughout the chapters; thus, the presentation of the sections is now complete.
The preceding discussion concludes; however, I shall now set forth separately the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) for specific practices.

Although the text of the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) already contains these matters in full, they are presented here because when the most urgent tasks arise—whether it be the task of generating goodness in those suited to the teaching, which is addressed in the section on receiving the precepts, or the task of extinguishing evil, which is addressed in the section on repenting the six classes of offenses—one must respond to them accordingly.

Since these [texts] have been mutually discussed and investigated, unless one is a scholar who has accumulated extensive learning, it would be extremely difficult to find and understand the *karmavācanā* within the thirty chapters.
"Single color" means there is no intermixture. Regarding the titles, the *Hanshu* states that they serve as a balance and scale;
thus, below, ten separate chapter titles are established, each weighed and ordered in sequence so as not to allow for confusion.

If the *Jiamojingzhu* (Commentary on the Karma Sūtra) is insufficiently clear regarding what is right or wrong and how practices are mutually manifested, one should refer to the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*).
This means that when classifying and discerning the commentaries of former masters, those that are incorrect are entirely discarded, while those that are correct are accepted;
such matters are clarified in the *Chao*.
From this point onward, the text concerns only the *karmavācanā*—the ritual procedures that serve as the enabling means—and the contemporary practices to which they apply;

these are further substantiated by citing sacred scriptures as evidence, all contained within the single fascicle of the *Karmavācanā*, for the purpose of aiding the world through practical application.

However, what follows below clarifies that there are two types of supplementation: textual and doctrinal. For instance, the citations from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and various other sutras and treatises constitute textual supplementation;
furthermore, the citation of the "seven fallacies" established according to their meaning constitutes doctrinal supplementation. Both of these will be fully elucidated in the respective sections.
It is regrettable that the traces of the ancients have been obscured.

Now, the *Karmavācanā* (Karma) is established as a chapter at the end; although it comprises as many as one hundred and eighty-four rules, all possess the merit of accomplishing tasks and benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, throughout the Vinaya, it is universally designated by the single term "Karma"—this is its definitive name.

Now, the intent of establishing this "Section on Correct Posture" is not merely to manifest humility; rather, it is because learning is what one preserves, and constant application refers to the matters that must be perpetually practiced.
(End of Commentary on the Preface to the *Karmavācanā Sūtra*)
On the first day of the fifth month in the first year of the Jianwu era, while following the sequence of the discourses in this volume, I wiped my aged eyes and added these dots;
I did so specifically for the sake of beginners who have not yet gained proficiency.
Śramaṇa Chengxin of E’ansi Temple (Total: 42; Births: 66)
